title: Incident Response, BCDR & Escalation Review - Acme Retail Systems
next_steps: Redwood: send SOC 2 Type II link and encryption/KMS matrix
Customer: share current DR RTO/RPO spreadsheet and pipeline SLA expectations
Schedule tabletop DR exercise with Acme execs for week of 2025-04-21
Redwood SE to provide runbook excerpt and PagerDuty escalation flow by 2025-04-12
action_items: Sophia Park | Send SOC 2 Type II report, ISO scoping note, and KMS matrix | 2025-04-12
Daniel Kim | Share excerpt of incident runbook (escalation flows + playbook) | 2025-04-12

Priya Shah | Confirm legal requirements for data residency for EU customers | 2025-04-18
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-10 15:00 PDT / Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Sophia Park (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Rhea Patel (Redwood CRE); Priya Shah (CISO - Acme), Miguel Torres (Head Infra), Liam O'Connor (Compliance), Dana Liu (Platform Ops), Ethan Brooks (SRE)

[00:00] Sophia Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call -- Sophia here, AE at Redwood. Dan and Rhea from the infra/ops side.
[00:15] Priya Shah: Hey all, Priya here. We have our infra and compliance folks on the call, want to make sure we cover incident response, BCDR expectations, and escalation.
[00:25] Daniel Kim: Great, thanks Priya. Today we want to walk through how Redwood handles incident detection, triage, escalation, RTO/RPO targets for both hosted and dedicated deployments, and what audit artifacts we can provide for your compliance team.
[00:40] Miguel Torres: Good. We run a hybrid stack; most of our workloads are in us-west on AWS but we have some EU data residency requirements for checkout data. We'll want to understand how Redwood's private deployment and network isolation options work with our VPC and KMS.
[00:55] Rhea Patel: Noted. We'll cover encryption at rest and in transit, KMS integration options (bring-your-own-key vs Redwood-managed), and what logs we can surface for your SIEM.
[01:10] Liam O'Connor: And from compliance, we need details on SOC 2 coverage for incident response and availability controls, plus evidence formats. Excel sheets are fine but we usually want PDFs of reports and system logs with timestamps.
[01:25] Sophia Park: We can share SOC 2 Type II report and an incident response summary. We'll also share a redacted runbook snippet for escalation.
[01:40] Ethan Brooks: Two quick context items: our RTO goal for payment flows is 15 minutes and RPO is 5 minutes; for product search it's 60/10. We need to know what Redwood guarantees or can commit to operationally.
[01:55] Daniel Kim: Understood. For hosted API, our platform-level target is 99.9% availability historically, but we have different service classes on Dedicated where you can define capacity and get SLA-backed uptime. For RTO/RPO during a severe incident we have two tiers: automated fallback (model variant fallback and region failover) for sub-minute continuity and a longer operator-driven recovery for full data plane failover.
[02:25] Dana Liu: Can you be concrete? If a primary region suffers a zone-wide outage, what's the expected time to failover to a secondary region for inference traffic and what's the expected data loss window?
[02:40] Daniel Kim: For stateless inference requests, traffic can be redirected in tens of seconds to a warm standby region if you use our cross-region routing and have an active duplicate config. For private deployments with KV cache or stateful shards, failover depends on whether you replicate the KV store. If you enable cross-region replication, typical RTO we've measured in tests is 8–20 minutes. RPO depends on replication frequency; with near-real-time async replication we see RPOs under a minute for critical keys, but for full KV stores it can be a few minutes.
[03:15] Miguel Torres: You mentioned warm standby — what's required from our side? Do we need to pre-provision capacity in the second region?
[03:25] Rhea Patel: Yes, you'll need reserved capacity in the secondary region for guaranteed throughput. Redwood can help size that. Alternatively, we have burst policies that can spin up capacity but that impacts RTO and could incur cold start latency.
[03:40] Priya Shah: Regarding escalation, who gets paged and what's the on-call rotation? We need names/roles to plug into our incident contact registry.
[03:50] Daniel Kim: Our standard is PagerDuty integration; primary on-call is our SRE rotation, then SE on-call for customer-impacting incidents. We can provide a redactable list of roles and escalation steps. For Dedicated customers we can establish a shared escalation bridge and named contacts.
[04:10] Ethan Brooks: How do you differentiate severity levels? Our taxonomy is sev0 (production down), sev1 (critical degradation), sev2 (partial impact). We need SLA credits mapped to these severities.
[04:25] Rhea Patel: We map Sev0/1 to immediate paging and separate runbooks. SLA credits are contract-defined; hosted customers typically see financial credits at 99.5/99.0 thresholds. For Dedicated, we negotiate higher SLAs based on reserved capacity. We'll surface the SLA table in the follow-up.
[04:45] Priya Shah: What about post-incident artifacts — timeline, root cause, mitigations, and evidence? We need a packet for audits.
[04:55] Daniel Kim: We produce a post-incident report with detailed timeline, logs (redacted), and mitigation steps. For customers on Dedicated or Private, we can include deeper forensic logs, subject to an agreed redaction policy.
[05:10] Miguel Torres: Logs — can you push them to our SIEM? We run Splunk and ingest via secure syslog or S3 ingestion.
[05:20] Rhea Patel: Yes, we can forward audit logs to a customer S3 bucket (encrypted) or integrate via syslog/HTTPS. We also expose structured audit APIs with event IDs to ingest into Splunk.
[05:35] Liam O'Connor: What retention windows do you offer by default? Compliance needs 1 year at minimum for some artifacts.
[05:45] Daniel Kim: Default audit log retention on hosted is 90 days. For enterprise add-on we can extend retention to 2 years and provide archival exports. For Private deployments, retention is whatever you configure locally.
[06:00] Sophia Park: Quick clarification — are you leaning toward Hosted, Dedicated, or Private for Acme?
[06:10] Priya Shah: We're evaluating Dedicated for core checkout flows and hosted for secondary features like internal productivity tooling. Data residency means dedicated instances for EU checkout shards.
[06:22] Daniel Kim: That mix aligns with common patterns. We'll outline a hybrid DR plan that covers region-level failover for hosted paths and a disaster recovery playbook for Dedicated clusters.
[06:35] Ethan Brooks: Encryption — KMS options. We need BYOK. We must have customer-controlled keys with rotation audit.
[06:45] Rhea Patel: We support AWS KMS customer-managed keys in VPC deployments. For hosted, we have Redwood-managed keys but can integrate with your KMS via an HSM/KMS bridge for some customers under an enterprise agreement. We'll document the options and the tradeoffs.
[06:58] Miguel Torres: If we bring our keys, can Redwood prove zero-knowledge access to plaintext? Our legal folks ask for attestations.
[07:10] Daniel Kim: We can provide architecture diagrams and access control statements showing that plaintext never leaves the compute instance except in memory; however, for full attestation you might require an on-prem or private deployment. We can also contractually define access controls and logging to satisfy legal.
[07:35] Dwight (off): [inaudible]...
[07:40] Priya Shah: Ok on RBAC and SSO — we use SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. We need role-based access controls for console and API keys, including token scoping.
[07:55] Rhea Patel: Redwood supports SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC. API keys can be scoped by model and rate limits; token-level audit trails are available. We'll share the RBAC matrix.
[08:10] Liam O'Connor: About audit logs — are admin actions logged (key rotations, role changes)? We need immutable logs for those events.
[08:20] Daniel Kim: Yes, admin-level events are logged with user, timestamp, and IP. For immutability we offer append-only storage backed by signed timestamps and can deliver SHA256 digests to your auditors on request.
[08:40] Ethan Brooks: On the topic of incident detection, what monitoring signals do you expose? We want latency percentiles, error rates, model degradation metrics, and internal health checks.
[08:55] Rhea Patel: We emit detailed telemetry: p50/p90/p99 latency, request error codes, backpressure indicators, KV cache hit rates, and model quality regressions. These can be sent to your metrics stack or visualized in Redwood Console.
[09:10] Miguel Torres: Regarding model fallbacks — if a model variant becomes unhealthy, is there automatic reroute to a lower-cost or lower-latency variant? How is that tested?
[09:22] Daniel Kim: Yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants; we run continuous health checks and have canary rollouts. We also run regular DR drills for Dedicated customers on request.
[09:35] Priya Shah: Let's talk about escalation paths in detail. Give us a sample runbook flow for a Sev0 production outage affecting checkout.
[09:45] Daniel Kim: (walks through) Step 1: Detection via health checks/alerting -> automatic traffic routing to warm standby. Step 2: PagerDuty paged for SRE (immediate), AE notified for customer comms. Step 3: SE and CRE join bridge for triage. Step 4: If cross-region failover needed, CRE initiates failover playbook. Step 5: Incident commander coordinates with customer named contacts for status updates.
[10:20] Rhea Patel: We also have pre-approved communications templates and we can provide a status page feed or webhook for your ops team.
[10:35] Ethan Brooks: What's the typical time to get an incident commander on a secure bridge call after detection?
[10:40] Daniel Kim: For Sev0 it's under 5 minutes to have an initial bridge; full command structure in 10–15 minutes.
[10:50] Miguel Torres: If the incident is due to a security compromise, do you have an IR retainer or third-party forensic partner?
[10:58] Rhea Patel: Yes, we have a cybersecurity forensics partner and can engage Mandiant-like services under our enterprise support packages. We also maintain chain-of-custody procedures for evidence.
[11:12] Priya Shah: For legal/audit, we need SLA remediation and credit calculation examples. Can you share a sample SLA schedule and historical uptime trends?
[11:22] Sophia Park: We'll attach a sample SLA schedule in the follow-up email and include historical uptime graphs for the last 6 months for our hosted service and Dedicated peer benchmarks.
[11:35] Liam O'Connor: On BCDR tabletop — we'll want Redwood to run a scenario: primary region down during peak load with PCI flow impacted. That will help us validate our checkout RTO.
[11:48] Daniel Kim: We can do that. We'll run a tabletop and optionally a live drill in a staging window. We'll prepare a scenario doc.
[12:00] Dana Liu: Are there any single points of failure in Redwood's control plane that could impact our control over failover or keys?
[12:10] Rhea Patel: Our control plane is geo-redundant. For Private deployments, the control plane can be customer-hosted. KMS keys are under your control if BYOK is used, so control-plane SLOs won't impact key availability.
[12:28] Miguel Torres: About runbooks: can you share both summary and full-level playbooks? We probably prefer redacted full ones.
[12:38] Daniel Kim: We'll share a redacted playbook excerpt with step-by-step commands and escalation contacts. Full playbooks require an NDA in some cases; we'll note that.
[12:50] Priya Shah: On metrics and SLOs — do you provide error budget alerts and policy-driven automated throttles?
[13:00] Rhea Patel: Yes, we integrate error-budget tracking and can enforce rate limiting or per-tenant throttles if configured. That helps protect critical tenants during incidents.
[13:12] Ethan Brooks: For payment flows, if you throttle due to noise, we need a bypass or prioritized lane. How is traffic prioritized?
[13:20] Daniel Kim: We support priority routing based on API key tiering and token-level priority. We can configure a prioritized queue for payment tokens to minimize disruption.
[13:35] Miguel Torres: Data residency again — in EU, logs must stay in EU for certain customers. How do you segregate cross-region logs?
[13:48] Rhea Patel: We can partition log storage by tenant and region. For EU checkout shards, audit logs and data can be stored in EU S3 buckets and we avoid replication out-of-region unless explicitly permitted.
[14:00] Priya Shah: Incident classification — we need to see the decision criteria for downgrading and closing incidents.
[14:10] Daniel Kim: We close incidents after full mitigation and a baseline restoration check; for outages we require a post-incident RCA with acceptance from the incident commander and relevant customer stakeholders. We'll include the closure checklist in the artifacts we provide.
[14:30] Sophia Park: Can we talk briefly about penetration testing and vulnerability disclosure?
[14:38] Rhea Patel: We do quarterly internal pentests and annual third-party tests; we publish a summary and maintain a vulnerability disclosure program. For dedicated/private deployments, we can coordinate a joint test.
[14:55] Priya Shah: If we find an issue, what's the expected patch timeline? Critical CVEs?
[15:05] Daniel Kim: Critical CVEs have a 48–72 hour mitigation target; patch windows vary by deployment but emergency patches are handled through our incident process. We'll provide our CVE response SLA in the follow-up.
[15:20] Liam O'Connor: Can Redwood sign a customer-specific incident SLA or a BCDR addendum?
[15:28] Sophia Park: Yes, for enterprise contracts we can add BCDR addenda with specific RTO/RPO commitments and audit deliverables. We'll have legal draft language after we align requirements.
[15:40] Miguel Torres: For Dedicated clusters, who has access to underlying nodes? We need to ensure access is limited to named engineers and logged.
[15:50] Rhea Patel: Access is RBAC-controlled with Just-In-Time SSH via our bastion and all sessions are recorded and auditable. We can export session recordings or hashes to your audit system.
[16:05] Daniel Kim: Also, for nodes we recommend using ephemeral credentials and enforce MFA for any admin operations.
[16:18] Ethan Brooks: On data exfil concerns, what's your process for investigating suspicious outbound traffic from a cluster?
[16:28] Rhea Patel: We have egress monitoring; upon detection we isolate the node, snapshot the disk, gather memory and network traces, and involve the IR partner if needed. Chain-of-custody and evidence packaging are part of that flow.
[16:45] Priya Shah: Let's capture a few concrete numbers for the notes: typical time to bridge for Sev0 under 5 minutes; CRE-led failover time for stateless under 1 minute; cross-region Dedicated failover typical 8–20 minutes. Please include these in your follow-up.
[17:00] Daniel Kim: Noted, we'll include those with caveats.
[17:08] Sophia Park: I want to flag a potential compliance ask: our procurement team may request continuous monitoring logs be sent into our AWS account. Is there an approach that avoids sending sensitive model prompts?
[17:20] Rhea Patel: We can redact user content from audit streams and only send metadata (request IDs, latencies, error codes). For customers needing full logs, a Private deployment is the recommended path.
[17:35] Miguel Torres: If we need full request-level logs for forensics, what's the storage and retrieval process?
[17:45] Daniel Kim: We can export full logs to your S3 for a configurable retention period; retrieval is via signed URLs or S3 access. We can also support encrypted archives with customer keys.
[17:58] Liam O'Connor: Are runbook and incident artifacts signed or timestamped to support audit trails?
[18:08] Rhea Patel: Yes, we can provide signed digests and appended audit certificates for incident reports.
[18:18] Priya Shah: Any dependencies on third-party services that could affect RTO? e.g., certificate authorities, KMS availability, cloud provider control plane outages?
[18:30] Daniel Kim: We minimize external attack surfaces; however, we do rely on cloud provider managed infra for hosted offerings. We design multi-region redundancy and explicit fallbacks for provider control plane disruptions, but those scenarios can extend RTO. We'll document the dependency matrix.
[18:50] Ethan Brooks: For change control and maintenance windows, how are planned downtimes communicated and do they affect SLA calculations?
[18:58] Rhea Patel: Planned maintenance is excluded from SLA calculations if notified within contractual windows. We have a maintenance calendar and provide advance notifications and post-maintenance reports.
[19:12] Miguel Torres: A question on backup validation: do you run periodic restores to validate backups?
[19:20] Daniel Kim: Yes, for Dedicated we run periodic backup-restore tests and can provide summary reports. For Hosted we do internal restore tests and publish results to enterprise customers on request.
[19:35] Priya Shah: For legal, we also need a list of all sub-processors and their regions. Can you provide that?
[19:45] Sophia Park: We'll attach the current sub-processor list and region map in the follow-up.
[19:55] Daniel Kim: Quick note on forensic evidence — some logs may contain PII; we follow data minimization for what we disclose and will coordinate redaction with Acme.
[20:10] Dana Liu: Is there a separate audit channel for urgent compliance questions? Sometimes we need a timely answer for legal holds.
[20:18] Sophia Park: We can set up a compliance contact and SLA for compliance questions; we'll flag a named Redwood compliance lead in the follow-up.
[20:28] Ethan Brooks: Regarding model retraining and data used, can you guarantee no customer data is used to train public models?
[20:38] Rhea Patel: We do not use customer prompts/outputs to train public models. We have a clear data usage policy and will include that doc.
[20:48] Miguel Torres: On testing failover — will you coordinate a shared maintenance window so we can run tests with our payment provider?
[20:58] Daniel Kim: Absolutely, we can coordinate and provide a pre/post checklist to minimize downstream impacts.
[21:10] Priya Shah: Anything else on business continuity?
[21:18] Daniel Kim: One more item: we maintain a standby capacity pool for emergencies; access is gated and can be included in your contract as a surge clause.
[21:30] Sophia Park: Great. Let's go to the recap and next steps.
[21:35] Sophia Park: Recap: Redwood to send SOC 2 Type II, KMS/encryption matrix, a redacted runbook excerpt, SLA sample, sub-processor list, and proposed tabletop scenario. Acme to share RTO/RPO table and decision on Dedicated sizing.
[21:55] Priya Shah: Sounds good. I'd like the tabletop week of 2025-04-21 if possible.
[22:05] Sophia Park: We'll propose two slots, one on 2025-04-22 and one on 2025-04-24.
[22:12] Daniel Kim: I'll draft a DR scenario doc and include measured failover timelines.
[22:20] Miguel Torres: We'll prepare our RTO/RPO spreadsheet and share by 2025-04-14.
[22:28] Rhea Patel: Action-wise, I'll prepare the runbook excerpt and the escalation flow diagram.
[22:35] Priya Shah: Thanks, all. Any final quick questions?
[22:40] Ethan Brooks: None here.
[22:43] Liam O'Connor: All good.
[22:46] Sophia Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with docs and next steps.
[22:52] End of meeting: informal post-call chat about scheduling (not transcribed in detail)

Notes: Transcript contains transcription noise; some names/autocaptures may be slightly off.

Attachments referenced: SOC2_TypeII_link (to be sent), RBAC_matrix.xlsx (to be sent), DR_scenario_doc (to be created), SLA_sample.pdf (to be sent).
